metadata.title: Recombinant Canine Coronaviruses in Dogs, Europe
metadata.digest_excerpt:
PubMed Trending #1
PMID: 20031041
Citation: Emerg Infect Dis. 2010 Jan;16(1):41-7. doi: 10.3201/eid1601.090726.

paper_text_source: Europe PMC PMC2874359 (full text), staged in the private papers repository as the Issue 144 bundle; doi 10.3201/eid1601.090726
verification_changes: Nadia said the recombinant had been reported as 'a couple more' strains in the United Kingdom; the paper gives no count for the UK strains (Erles and Brownlie, ref. 15), so the number is cut.

Nadia called the oldest archival recombinant 'about four years before anyone reported the subtype at all'; the paper says four years before it was reported in Italy, and the script itself describes strain UCD1, reported about twenty years earlier.
Nadia called the two CCoV genotypes 'near-identical across the genome'; the paper reports they share up to 96% nucleotide identity, an upper bound, so 'closely related' replaces it.

Theo's takeaway said the one-in-five average was 'almost entirely Hungary'; Hungary supplies 31 of the 78 CCoV-IIb samples and Italy 34, so the honest statement is that dropping Hungary leaves the rest of Europe near an eighth (47/368, 12.8%) — same correction in show-notes takeaway 1, and Nadia's 'hiding almost everything' softened to 'hiding a lot'.

Nadia described the ORF7a/7b control as run on 'twenty recombinant-positive samples' without the selection: the paper ran it on 20 samples positive for CCoV-IIb and negative for CCoV-I, now said out loud.
Trimmed the cold open's 're-read' aside to pay for the added clauses without going over the spoken-length ceiling.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo. This is the Friday pick, so it's whatever has been most discussed on PubMed this week rather than anything we chose.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And at the top was a paper called Recombinant Canine Coronaviruses in Dogs, Europe, in Emerging Infectious Diseases — from twenty ten. They screened more than a thousand faecal samples from dogs with acute diarrhoea, across fourteen European countries, for one hybrid virus: a dog coronavirus carrying a stretch of a pig coronavirus.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. So why is that worth ten minutes? A hybrid virus in dogs sounds like veterinary housekeeping. What's the claim?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hmm. The honest answer is that it's a counting paper, and the counting had never been done. Before this, the recombinant was a handful of isolates — four strains in Italy, and others from the United Kingdom. Nobody knew whether it was a freezer curiosity or established in dogs. The authors say it outright: nobody had determined the prevalence of this subtype.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right, a different contribution from a mechanism paper. Then set up the virology, because "dog virus carrying pig virus" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: So. One antigenic group holds the pig virus, transmissible gastroenteritis virus, the cat coronavirus and the dog one. They're so close that the taxonomy committee's own proposal was to call them host-range variants of a single species — above ninety-six percent identical in the main replicase domains.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm. So the species boundary is mostly about which animal you found it in.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Largely. The gene that does differ is the spike, the surface protein that binds the host cell — also the one antibodies mostly see. Dog coronavirus comes in two types, closely related across the genome but strongly divergent in spike. And in some type two viruses, the first stretch of that gene — the part making the outward-facing tip — is the pig virus version instead. The rest is still a dog virus. That's the subtype they call two-b; the classical ones are two-a.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay, I can hold that. So the central claim is that two-b is widespread?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That it's circulating, in multiple countries, at a share of infections you can't dismiss. They get there with a P-C-R built to exploit that divergence: one primer upstream in a conserved region, then forward into either the classical dog spike or the pig-type one. Whichever reaction amplifies gives you the subtype.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hold on. That's clean, but the subtype call is then the presence or absence of a band. Those assays fail silently when a primer site drifts — and the premise is that this region is where the variation lives. What happens to a strain whose front end is neither sequence?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's invisible, and the paper doesn't test for that. They sequence what amplifies, which confirms the positives, but a negative isn't evidence of absence — and that matters most where they report nothing.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is where exactly? Give me the shape of the result.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: One thousand one hundred seventy-two samples. Just over forty-two percent carried any dog coronavirus. Of those, roughly a fifth were type one alone, a bit under half type two alone, and the rest — call it a third — had both at once.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: A third carrying both. That's a lot of co-infection.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is, though the authors note it's fewer mixed infections than earlier studies reported, not more. Then, within the samples containing type two, about one in five carried the recombinant. Seventy-eight of four hundred.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: A fifth. And how is it distributed? An average across Europe is usually hiding something.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's hiding a lot. Hungary is thirty-one of thirty-two. The United Kingdom is about a quarter, Italy about an eighth, then single strains from Greece, Romania and Sweden, and nothing from the rest.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh — so "a fifth of type two infections in Europe" is one country at saturation plus a long tail. Near-total in Hungary says something local: a trade route, a kennel network. One in eight in Italy says endemic and slow. The European average is the one I'd throw away.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed, and the sample counts make that worse rather than better. Of the whole set, over sixty percent came from Italy. Poland and Slovenia contributed one sample each — and both were positive, which the text writes up as a hundred percent.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is not a prevalence, it's a coin landing once. And Hungary's thirty-one comes out of, what, about forty samples from that country?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Around forty. So the headline is solid as an existence proof and thin as an estimate. In fairness, these samples arrived at a diagnostic lab over eight years. It was never a survey, and they don't claim it was.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And every dog in here already has acute diarrhoea, with no healthy-dog arm anywhere in the paper. So nothing tells me whether carrying the recombinant makes a dog ill.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nothing in it can. The one piece of evidence on severity comes from a previous study, not this one — experimental infection of coronavirus-seronegative beagle pups, where the recombinant did what the classical strains do. Mild diarrhoea, a few days, no systemic spread. A new front end, not a new disease.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hmm, and one more thing the subtype call isn't. The screening assay quantifies virus, and the loads span orders of magnitude, so a positive covers anything from a trace to a flood. But the subtyping is a band on a gel. Nothing here tells you how much recombinant virus a dog was shedding — which is the quantity you'd want if you were asking whether it spreads well.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then let's do the recombination claim, because that's the part that could be an artefact. If pig and dog sequence turn up in one reaction, the boring explanation is that these dogs were shedding actual pig virus — they eat things.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right, and the control for that is the best thing in the paper. The genomes end differently: dog and cat viruses carry two small accessory genes there, the pig virus one. So one P-C-R across that region gives a short product from pig virus and a much longer one from dog viruses. They ran it on twenty of the recombinant-positive samples, the ones with no type one in them.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: All twenty gave the long product. These are dog viruses carrying a pig-type spike tip, not pig viruses in a dog.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm. It's a size readout, not a sequence, so it rules out the one thing it was built to rule out. But it's the right experiment, it's cheap, and plenty of papers would have skipped it. What does the sequencing add?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They picked twenty-six strains across the regions, sequenced both ends of the spike gene, and got reads from all but two. At the front end these strains sit around eighty percent identical to the pig virus, and only in the mid-thirties to classical dog type two.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. Mid-thirties is barely alignable. That's not drift, that's a different gene in that slot.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the whole argument in one comparison. And then at the back end of the same gene, the same strains are above ninety percent identical to classical dog type two. One virus, two different ancestries, with the join inside a single gene.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Although — careful. At the back end, how close are the pig viruses to the classical dog ones anyway? If they're also high there, that comparison isn't discriminating much, and the front-end flip carries the claim alone.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They're close. Upper eighties to low nineties for the pig virus, against low to high nineties for the dog one. So the back end only tells you the backbone is dog-like; the front end forces the recombination reading. Which is how the authors frame it too.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Fine. I'll take recombinant. Now the geography. What's the evidence for a route?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Tree topology. The British strains form their own cluster, while the Italian and eastern European ones are mixed together. The authors read that as dog movement, and point to heavy importation of dogs into Italy, plus two precedents in the same corridor — canine infectious hepatitis, and one lineage of canine distemper.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So the mechanism is borrowed from other papers and the data is a topology. That's a hypothesis consistent with the tree, not a route. And with sampling this uneven you'd get clustering by country from collection alone.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's fair. Though the piece I found genuinely interesting isn't about geography. There's an old pig-type dog strain described about twenty years before this paper — and at the front of spike it sits with the pig viruses, not with these European ones.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Ah, okay. So that's not one recombination event spreading. That's the same swap happening more than once, at different times.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's their reading, and I think it holds. The archival screening pushes the European ones back too: the oldest recombinant in the stored samples is from two thousand one, about four years before the subtype was reported in Italy.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is the useful kind of freezer result. It wasn't emerging when it was noticed; it was already there. Where does that leave the vaccine line?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Carefully worded, and worth reading exactly. They say the genetic distance in spike questions the efficacy of vaccines based on classical strains. Not that vaccines fail. Then they add the thing I'd credit them for: only vaccination trials with challenge by recombinant strains could assess it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Good. The chain from "the spike tip is divergent" to "dogs are unprotected" has at least two unmeasured links, and the cross-reactivity data they lean on is from another study. It's a reason to run the trial, not a finding that vaccines fail.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And this connects to something we keep running into: a prevalence number built on a sample that was never drawn for the question. In episode eighty-two, the rabies undercount, it was deceased organ donors standing in for everyone who dies. Here it's diagnostic submissions standing in for dogs in Europe.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And the difference is instructive. That paper carried its load-bearing assumption on the surface and quantified what would break it. This one doesn't argue the sampling frame at all — it reports what came in, country by country, and leaves you to notice that one country supplied two thirds of it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So, my verdict. It's the first prevalence estimate for this subtype anywhere, against a base of a few isolates — on that comparison it moved the field. But it's a convenience sample, so what it establishes is that the recombinant is established, not how common it is. And it can't support the vaccine worry it raises.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm. I'd add that the controls are better than the sampling. The gene-end assay and sequencing both ends were the right calls, and a lot of surveillance work of this vintage would have reported the band and stopped.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then three takeaways. One: in dogs with diarrhoea across Europe, about a fifth of type two infections carried the pig-type spike tip — but drop Hungary, at thirty-one of thirty-two, and the rest of Europe is nearer an eighth. Two: the recombination is solid, because the front of the spike gene matches the pig virus far better than the classical dog version, and a gene-end control rules out pig virus in the samples. Three: the vaccine worry is a hypothesis, and the authors say so.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: What I'd watch for is a sample set that includes dogs without diarrhoea. If the recombinant turns up at the same rate in healthy animals, this stops being a disease story and becomes an ecology one — and that changes what the Hungarian number means.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'd watch for the trial they name. Vaccinate with the classical strain, challenge with the recombinant, count sick dogs. If protection holds, the spike distance was a sequence fact with no clinical consequence. If it doesn't, this paper was the early warning, sitting in the literature for years.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The paper is in Emerging Infectious Diseases, twenty ten. Thanks for listening to Science TLDR.
